claim: Neurons in macaque premotor cortex show firing rate modulation whether the subject performs an action or observes another individual performing a similar action.
source: Neurons in macaque premotor cortex show firing rate modulation whether the subject performs an action or observes another individual performing a similar action.
evidence: This is a general statement about mirror neurons supported by the broader literature and the study's own findings.

claim: Many, if not most, mirror neurons show noncongruent activity during execution and observation.
source: Although such mirror neurons have been thought to have highly congruent discharge during execution and observation, many, if not most, show noncongruent activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and the study's own findings.

claim: Low-dimensional neural trajectories of reaching movements exhibit comparatively simple dynamical motifs.
source: Studies of reaching movements, for which low-dimensional neural trajectories exhibit comparatively simple dynamical motifs, have shown that these prevalent patterns of co-modulation pass through subspaces which are shared in part, but in part are visited exclusively during either execution or observation.
evidence: This is supported by references to prior studies on reaching movements.

claim: Patterns of co-modulation during reaching movements pass through subspaces which are shared in part, but in part are visited exclusively during either execution or observation.
source: Studies of reaching movements, for which low-dimensional neural trajectories exhibit comparatively simple dynamical motifs, have shown that these prevalent patterns of co-modulation pass through subspaces which are shared in part, but in part are visited exclusively during either execution or observation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The neural dynamics of hand movements are more complex than those of reaching movements.
source: The neural dynamics of hand movements are more complex, however.
evidence: This is supported by the context of the study and references to prior work.

claim: Instantaneous neural subspaces most often remained distinct during execution versus observation.
source: These instantaneous neural subspaces most often remained distinct during execution versus observation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data presented in Figures 7 and related analyses.

claim: Latent dynamics during execution and observation could be partially aligned with canonical correlation, indicating some similarity of the relationships among neural representations of different movements relative to one another during execution and observation.
source: Nevertheless, latent dynamics during execution and observation could be partially aligned with canonical correlation, indicating some similarity of the relationships among neural representations of different movements relative to one another during execution and observation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the canonical correlation analysis presented in Figure 8.

claim: During action execution, mirror neurons showed consistent patterns of co-modulation both within and between sessions.
source: We also found that during action execution, mirror neurons showed consistent patterns of co-modulation both within and between sessions, but other non-mirror neurons that were modulated only during action execution and not during observation showed considerable variability of co-modulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the within-group and between-session canonical correlation analyses presented in Figure 8.

claim: Non-mirror neurons that were modulated only during action execution and not during observation showed considerable variability of co-modulation.
source: We also found that during action execution, mirror neurons showed consistent patterns of co-modulation both within and between sessions, but other non-mirror neurons that were modulated only during action execution and not during observation showed considerable variability of co-modulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the within-group canonical correlation analyses for AE neurons presented in Figure 8D.

claim: Neurons in ventral premotor cortex (PMv) discharge during both execution and observation of movements.
source: Such neurons have been found in the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) (Maranesi et al., 2014; Gallese et al., 1996), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) (Cisek and Kalaska, 2004; Papadourakis and Raos, 2019; Albertini et al., 2021; Pezzulo et al., 2022), and M1 (Dushanova and Donoghue, 2010; Kraskov et al., 2014; Vigneswaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Neurons in dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) discharge during both execution and observation of movements.
source: Such neurons have been found in the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) (Maranesi et al., 2014; Gallese et al., 1996), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) (Cisek and Kalaska, 2004; Papadourakis and Raos, 2019; Albertini et al., 2021; Pezzulo et al., 2022), and M1 (Dushanova and Donoghue, 2010; Kraskov et al., 2014; Vigneswaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Neurons in M1 discharge during both execution and observation of movements.
source: Such neurons have been found in the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) (Maranesi et al., 2014; Gallese et al., 1996), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) (Cisek and Kalaska, 2004; Papadourakis and Raos, 2019; Albertini et al., 2021; Pezzulo et al., 2022), and M1 (Dushanova and Donoghue, 2010; Kraskov et al., 2014; Vigneswaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The prevalence of execution/observation neurons in cortical motor areas argues against their activity during observation being merely an epiphenomenon unrelated to their activity during execution.
source: The prevalence of such execution/observation neurons in cortical motor areas argues against their activity during observation being merely an epiphenomenon unrelated to their activity during execution but also poses a larger question: What is the nature of the relationship between their activity during execution versus observation?
evidence: This is an inference based on the prevalence of mirror neurons.

claim: Early studies of mirror neurons emphasized those with congruent discharge during execution and observation contexts.
source: Early studies of these neurons emphasized those with congruent discharge during execution and observation contexts.
evidence: This is supported by the historical context and citations to early mirror neuron studies.

claim: Congruent neurons discharged during the same type of grasp during both execution and observation.
source: Congruent neurons discharged during the same type of grasp (Gallese et al., 1996; Rizzolatti et al., 1996) or retained the same preferred direction (Dushanova and Donoghue, 2010; Kilner and Lemon, 2013) during both execution and observation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Congruent neurons retained the same preferred direction during both execution and observation.
source: Congruent neurons discharged during the same type of grasp (Gallese et al., 1996; Rizzolatti et al., 1996) or retained the same preferred direction (Dushanova and Donoghue, 2010; Kilner and Lemon, 2013) during both execution and observation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Emphasis on congruent neurons led to the notion that they mediate understanding of observed actions as they mirror their own activity during execution.
source: Emphasis on such congruent neurons led to the notion that they mediate understanding of observed actions as they mirror their own activity during execution (di Pellegrino et al., 1992; Rizzolatti and Craighero, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work on mirror neurons.

claim: Early studies also reported many noncongruent neurons that discharged during execution and during observation but discharged differently in the two contexts.
source: In addition to congruent neurons, however, even early studies also reported many other noncongruent neurons that also discharged during execution and during observation but discharged differently in the two contexts (Gallese et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an early mirror neuron study.

claim: In many studies, roughly half or more of the neurons modulated during both execution and observation were noncongruent.
source: In many studies, roughly half or more of the neurons modulated during both execution and observation were noncongruent (Dushanova and Donoghue, 2010; Kraskov et al., 2014; Mazurek et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Of PMv neurons modulated during both execution and observation, over the time course of behavioral trials, only ~20% showed brief periods with strictly congruent firing rates.
source: Of PMv neurons modulated during both execution and observation, over the time course of behavioral trials, only ~20% showed brief periods with strictly congruent firing rates (Pomper et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: In both PMv and PMd, the proportion of congruent neurons may not be different from that expected by chance alone.
source: And in both PMv and PMd, the proportion of congruent neurons may not be different from that expected by chance alone (Papadourakis and Raos, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Multiple studies have found that of the neurons in cortical motor areas that are modulated during execution, a large fraction are also modulated during observation.
source: Nevertheless, multiple studies have found that of the neurons in cortical motor areas that are modulated during execution, a large fraction are also modulated during observation.
evidence: This is supported by the context and citations to prior studies.

claim: 31 of 64 (49%) pyramidal tract neurons in PMv showed modulation during both execution and observation.
source: For example, 31 of 64 (49%) pyramidal tract neurons in PMv and 65 of 132 (49%) in M1 showed modulation during both execution and observation (Kraskov et al., 2009; Vigneswaran et al., 2013; Kraskov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: 65 of 132 (49%) pyramidal tract neurons in M1 showed modulation during both execution and observation.
source: For example, 31 of 64 (49%) pyramidal tract neurons in PMv and 65 of 132 (49%) in M1 showed modulation during both execution and observation (Kraskov et al., 2009; Vigneswaran et al., 2013; Kraskov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The observation-related activity of execution-related neurons in PMv, PMd, and M1 is somehow related to the motoric functions of these cortical areas.
source: Such findings suggest that the observation-related activity of execution-related neurons in PMv, PMd, and M1, some of which project to the spinal cord, is somehow related to the motoric functions of these cortical areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on the prevalence of mirror neurons and their anatomical projections.

claim: Behavior evolving in time may be represented more accurately by the temporal progression of co-modulation in populations of neurons than by the temporal pattern of firing rate in single neurons.
source: Behavior evolving in time may be represented more accurately by the temporal progression of co-modulation in populations of neurons than by the temporal pattern of firing rate in single neurons (Shenoy et al., 2013; Cunningham and Yu, 2014; Vyas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work on population coding.

claim: Patterns of co-modulation can be considered in a high-dimensional neural-state space where the firing rate of each neuron is a separate, orthogonal dimension.
source: Patterns of co-modulation can be considered in a high-dimensional neural-state space where the firing rate of each neuron is a separate, orthogonal dimension.
evidence: This is a standard conceptual framework in computational neuroscience.

claim: The instantaneous, simultaneous firing rates of all N neurons form a point in neural state space, and the time series of these instantaneous points traces out a neural trajectory over time.
source: The instantaneous, simultaneous firing rates of all N neurons then form a point in this space, and the time series of these instantaneous points traces out a neural trajectory over time.
evidence: This is a standard conceptual framework in computational neuroscience.

claim: Neural population trajectories do not visit all regions of the N-dimensional state space equivalently.
source: Neural population trajectories do not visit all regions of the N-dimensional state space equivalently, however.
evidence: This is supported by prior studies on neural population dynamics.

claim: Dimensionality reduction techniques can be used to identify a small set of latent dimensions—a subspace—that captures the most prevalent patterns of co-modulation among the population of N neurons.
source: Dimensionality reduction techniques can be used to identify a small set of latent dimensions—a subspace—that captures the most prevalent patterns of co-modulation among the population of N neurons.
evidence: This is a standard approach in computational neuroscience.

claim: Rotational motifs in a low-dimensional subspace capture much of the neural population's firing rate variance during reaching movements made with the arm.
source: Studies of neural trajectories underlying action execution that focused on reaching movements made with the arm have revealed that rotational motifs in a low-dimensional subspace capture much of the neural population's firing rate variance (Churchland et al., 2012; Russo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The M1 neural trajectories underlying grasping movements are more complex than those underlying reaching movements.
source: But the M1 neural trajectories underlying grasping movements (Suresh et al., 2020) or force production at the wrist (Dekleva et al., 2024) are more complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The M1 neural trajectories underlying force production at the wrist are more complex than those underlying reaching movements.
source: But the M1 neural trajectories underlying grasping movements (Suresh et al., 2020) or force production at the wrist (Dekleva et al., 2024) are more complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The latent subspaces that capture the predominant patterns of co-modulation among M1 neurons shift progressively over the time course of behavioral trials involving reaching for, grasping, and manipulating various objects at various locations.
source: The latent subspaces that capture the predominant patterns of co-modulation among M1 neurons, for example, shift progressively over the time course of behavioral trials involving reaching for, grasping, and manipulating various objects at various locations (Rouse and Schieber, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The variance in neural activity averaged across all the conditions in a given task context is condition-independent.
source: The variance in neural activity averaged across all the conditions in a given task context is condition-independent.
evidence: This is a definition of condition-independent variance.

claim: Subtracting condition-independent activity from the unit's firing rate during each trial gives the remaining variance, and averaging separately across trials in each condition gives the condition-dependent variance.
source: Subtracting this condition-independent activity from the unit's firing rate during each trial gives the remaining variance, and averaging separately across trials in each of the eight directions then averages out noise variance, leaving the condition-dependent variance that represents the unit's modulation among the eight directions (conditions).
evidence: This describes a method for partitioning variance.

claim: Condition-independent, condition-dependent, and noise variance can be partitioned through demixed principal component analysis (PCA).
source: Alternatively, condition-independent, condition-dependent, and noise variance can be partitioned through demixed principal component analysis (PCA) (Kobak et al., 2016; Gallego et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior methodological work.

claim: The extent to which neural dynamics occur in a subspace shared by execution and observation versus subspaces unique to execution or observation may differ for the condition-independent versus condition-dependent partitions of neural activity.
source: The extent to which neural dynamics occur in a subspace shared by execution and observation versus subspaces unique to execution or observation may differ for the condition-independent versus condition-dependent partitions of neural activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior work and the study's rationale.

claim: The condition-dependent activity of PM MN populations progresses through distinct subspaces during execution versus observation.
source: Here, we tested the hypothesis that the condition-dependent activity of PM MN populations progresses through distinct subspaces during execution versus observation, which would indicate distinct patterns of co-modulation among MNs during execution versus observation.
evidence: This is the primary hypothesis tested in the study, supported by the data presented.

claim: The condition-dependent subspace shifts progressively over the time course of behavioral trials.
source: We then tested the hypothesis that the condition-dependent subspace shifts progressively over the time course of behavioral trials (Figure 1A) by calculating the principal angles between four selected instantaneous subspaces that occurred at times easily defined in each behavioral trial—instruction onset (I), go cue (G), movement onset (M), and the beginning of the final hold (H)—and every other instantaneous subspace in the time series.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study, supported by the data in Figure 4.

claim: Condition-dependent neural trajectories for the four RGM movements tended to separate increasingly over the course of behavioral trials.
source: Initial analyses showed that condition-dependent neural trajectories for the four RGM movements tended to separate increasingly over the course of behavioral trials.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by the data in Figure 5.

claim: Three sessions were recorded from each of the three monkeys, R, F, and T.
source: Three sessions were recorded from each of the three monkeys, R, F, and T (a 6 kg female, 10 kg male, and 10 kg male, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Monkey R was a 6 kg female.
source: Three sessions were recorded from each of the three monkeys, R, F, and T (a 6 kg female, 10 kg male, and 10 kg male, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Monkey F was a 10 kg male.
source: Three sessions were recorded from each of the three monkeys, R, F, and T (a 6 kg female, 10 kg male, and 10 kg male, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Monkey T was a 10 kg male.
source: Three sessions were recorded from each of the three monkeys, R, F, and T (a 6 kg female, 10 kg male, and 10 kg male, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The RGM components were not performed separately, but rather in a continuous fluid motion during the movement epoch of the task sequence.
source: Because we chose to study relatively naturalistic movements, the RGM components were not performed separately, but rather in a continuous fluid motion during the movement epoch of the task sequence (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral task.

claim: Joint kinematics, EMG activity, and neuron activity in the M1 all vary throughout the movement epoch in relation to both reach location and object grasped, with location predominating early in the movement epoch and object predominating later.
source: In previous studies involving a version of this task without separate instruction and delay epochs, we have shown that joint kinematics, EMG activity, and neuron activity in the M1 all vary throughout the movement epoch in relation to both reach location and object grasped, with location predominating early in the movement epoch and object predominating later (Rouse and Schieber, 2015; Rouse and Schieber, 2016a; Rouse and Schieber, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies by the authors.

claim: The present task did not dissociate the reach, the hand shape used to grasp the object, and the manipulation performed on the object.
source: The present task, however, did not dissociate the reach, the hand shape used to grasp the object, and the manipulation performed on the object.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral task design.

claim: The three monkeys each were implanted with floating microelectrode arrays (FMAs) in the PMv and in the PMd.
source: The three monkeys each were implanted with floating microelectrode arrays (FMAs, Microprobes for Life Sciences) in the PMv and in the PMd.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A large fraction of condition-dependent neural variance during reaching movements without grasping can be captured in a two-dimensional subspace.
source: Whereas a large fraction of condition-dependent neural variance during reaching movements without grasping can be captured in a two-dimensional subspace (Churchland et al., 2012; Ames et al., 2014), condition-dependent activity in movements that involve grasping is more complex (Suresh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Condition-dependent activity in movements that involve grasping is more complex than in reaching movements without grasping.
source: Whereas a large fraction of condition-dependent neural variance during reaching movements without grasping can be captured in a two-dimensional subspace (Churchland et al., 2012; Ames et al., 2014), condition-dependent activity in movements that involve grasping is more complex (Suresh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The greater complexity of grasping movements may reflect the greater complexity of controlling the 24 degrees of freedom (DOFs) in the hand and wrist as compared to the 4 DOFs in the elbow and shoulder.
source: In part, this may reflect the greater complexity of controlling the 24 degrees of freedom (DOFs) in the hand and wrist as compared to the 4 DOFs in the elbow and shoulder (Sobinov and Bensmaia, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior work on hand biomechanics.

claim: Most of the variance in the four object-specific neural trajectories is comprised of a shared rotational component.
source: Most of the variance in these four trajectories is comprised of a shared rotational component.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The condition-independent activity is reflected by the black trajectory obtained by averaging trajectories from trials involving all four objects together.
source: The black trajectory, obtained by averaging trajectories from trials involving all four objects together, represents this condition-independent (i.e. independent of the object involved) activity.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The condition-dependent variation in activity is reflected by the variation in the colored trajectories around the black trajectory.
source: The condition-dependent (i.e. dependent on which object was involved) variation in activity is reflected by the variation in the colored trajectories around the black trajectory.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The condition-dependent trajectories appear knotted rather than exhibiting a simple rotational motif.
source: Rather than exhibiting a simple rotational motif, these trajectories appear knotted.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After instruction onset (I), the instantaneous subspace shifted quickly away from the subspace at time I.
source: Figure 4A shows that after instruction onset (I), the instantaneous subspace shifted quickly away from the subspace at time I, indicated by a rapid increase in principal angle to levels not much lower than what might be expected by chance alone (horizontal dashed line).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Throughout the remainder of the instruction and delay epochs (from I to G), the 80-trial instantaneous subspace shifted gradually and concurrently toward the all-trial subspaces that would be reached at the end of the delay period (G) and then at the onset of movement (M).
source: In contrast, throughout the remainder of the instruction and delay epochs (from I to G), Figure 4B and C show that the 80-trial instantaneous subspace shifted gradually and concurrently, not sequentially, toward the all-trial subspaces that would be reached at the end of the delay period (G) and then at the onset of movement (M), indicated by the progressive decreases in principal angle.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Shifting toward the H subspace did not begin until the movement onset (M).
source: As shown by Figure 4D, shifting toward the H subspace did not begin until the movement onset (M).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The temporal progression of the MN instantaneous subspace during observation was similar to that found during execution, particularly around times I and H.
source: Overall, the temporal progression of the MN instantaneous subspace during observation was similar to that found during execution, particularly around times I and H.
evidence: This is supported by comparing the data in Figures 4A-D with 4E-H.

claim: The decrease in principal angle relative to the G and M instantaneous subspaces during the delay epoch was less pronounced during observation than during execution.
source: The decrease in principal angle relative to the G and M instantaneous subspaces during the delay epoch was less pronounced during observation than during execution.
evidence: This is supported by comparing the data in Figures 4B-C with 4F-G.

claim: During execution, the AE populations had a pattern of gradual decrease in principal angle similar to that found in the MN population.
source: During execution, however, Figure 4I–L shows that the AE populations had a pattern of gradual decrease in principal angle similar to that found in the MN population (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by comparing the data in Figures 4I-L with 4A-D.

claim: The trajectory segments for each of the four objects sampled at different times were distinct when projected into each instantaneous subspace.
source: Rather than appearing knotted as in Figure 3, these short trajectory segments are distinct when projected into each instantaneous subspace.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: During execution, the trajectory segments for the four objects were close together at the time of instruction onset (I), became more separated at the time of the go cue (G), had separated further still at movement onset (M), and had become somewhat less separated at the beginning of the final hold (H).
source: Along the main diagonal of Figure 5A, each set of trajectory segments is projected into its corresponding subspace, showing that during execution the trajectory segments for the four objects were close together at the time of instruction onset (I), became more separated at the time of the go cue (G), had separated further still at movement onset (M), and had become somewhat less separated at the beginning of the final hold (H).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: During observation, a similar trend of increasing trajectory separation is evident along the main diagonal, although the separation is less than during execution.
source: During observation (Figure 5B), a similar trend is evident along the main diagonal, although the separation is less, reflecting the commonly described lower firing rates of MNs during observation than during execution (Ferroni et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to prior work.

claim: During observation, the separation of the four trajectories was somewhat greater at the beginning of the hold (H) than at movement onset (M).
source: In addition, during observation, the separation of the four trajectories was somewhat greater at the beginning of the hold (H) than at movement onset (M).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Classification accuracy consistently peaked at a time point within or near the 100 ms duration of the corresponding trajectory segments.
source: As might have been expected based both on principal angles and on trajectory separation, classification accuracy consistently peaked at a time point within or near the 100 ms duration of the corresponding trajectory segments (orange flags at the top of the vertical lines).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Classification accuracy decreased progressively at times preceding and following each peak.
source: Classification accuracy decreased progressively at times preceding and following each of these peaks.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mean classification of the instruction trajectory segments initially was ~0.25, rose toward ~0.50 around the time of the instruction onset, and then fell back to ~0.25.
source: In monkey R, mean classification of the instruction trajectory segments (Figure 6A) initially was ~0.25, rose toward ~0.50 around the time of the instruction onset, and then fell back to ~0.25.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mean accuracy for the go segments began at ~0.25, rose gradually during the delay epoch to peak at ~0.75 around the time of the go cue, and decreased thereafter.
source: Mean accuracy for the go segments (Figure 6B) also began at ~0.25, rose gradually during the delay epoch to peak at ~0.75 around the time of the go cue, and decreased thereafter.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: For the movement and hold segments, classification accuracy started somewhat higher and peaked at ~0.90.
source: For the movement (Figure 6C) and hold (Figure 6D) segments, classification accuracy started somewhat higher (reflecting greater trajectory segment separation at the time they were clipped, Figure 5) and peaked at ~0.90.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Classification accuracy of movement trajectory segments rose steadily from the second half of the delay epoch through the reaction epoch, peaked above chance levels shortly after movement onset (M), and fell back to near baseline during the movement epoch (M to H).
source: Movement segment classification accuracy rose steadily from the second half of the delay epoch through the reaction epoch (G to M), peaked above chance levels shortly after movement onset (M), and fell back to near baseline during the movement epoch (M to H).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The progressive increase in classification accuracy of movement trajectory segments during the preparatory delay and reaction epochs indicates that as these epochs proceeded, the condition-dependent neural trajectories of PM MNs shifted gradually, not abruptly, toward where they would be at movement onset.
source: The progressive increase in classification accuracy of movement trajectory segments during the preparatory delay and reaction epochs indicates that as these epochs proceeded, the condition-dependent neural trajectories of PM MNs shifted gradually, not abruptly, toward where they would be at movement onset.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: During execution trials, classification accuracy for AE populations showed a time course quite similar to that for MN populations, though amplitudes were lower overall.
source: During execution trials, classification accuracy for AE populations (Figure 6I–L) showed a time course quite similar to that for MN populations, though amplitudes were lower overall, most likely because of the smaller population sizes.
evidence: This is supported by comparing the data in Figures 6I-L with 6A-D.

claim: Throughout the time course of trials in monkeys R and F, the instantaneous execution and observation condition-dependent subspaces showed little, if any, overlap.
source: Although monkey T did show evidence of some degree of overlap (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), throughout the time course of trials in monkeys R and F, the instantaneous execution and observation condition-dependent subspaces showed little, if any, overlap.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: When both sets of trajectory segments are projected into another common subspace identified with CCA, a similar relationship among the neural representations of the four movements during execution and observation is revealed.
source: But when both sets of trajectory segments are projected into another common subspace identified with CCA, as shown in Figure 8B, a similar relationship among the neural representations of the four movements during execution and observation is revealed.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: PM MN populations showed some degree of similarity in the relationships among their latent dynamic representations of the four RGM movements during execution and observation, particularly at the time of the hold.
source: PM MN populations thus showed some degree of similarity in the relationships among their latent dynamic representations of the four RGM movements during execution and observation, particularly at the time of the hold.
evidence: This is supported by the CCA data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The alignment of AE neuron execution trajectory segments with those of the simultaneously recorded MN population was weaker than the alignment of MN trajectories during execution versus observation.
source: Surprisingly, the alignment of AE neuron execution trajectory segments with those of the simultaneously recorded MN population was weaker than the alignment of MN trajectories during execution versus observation.
evidence: This is supported by comparing the data in Figure 8C (blue vs. red).

claim: The MN/AE coefficients were significantly lower than the corresponding MN/1:2 coefficients in all 9 cases.
source: Post hoc testing showed that in all significant cases (9 cases: 3 CCA coefficients × 3 sets of trajectory segments, Tukey's honestly significant difference tests), though the MN:E/O coefficients might not be significantly lower than the corresponding MN/1:2 coefficients and/or significantly higher than the MN/AE coefficients, the MN/AE coefficients were significantly lower than the corresponding MN/1:2 coefficients in all 9 cases.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: The patterns of co-modulation among AE neurons during the four different RGM movements did not align with the patterns of co-modulation among MNs.
source: These findings fail to support the hypothesis that during action execution, MN and AE neuron trajectory segments would align well and suggest instead that the patterns of co-modulation among AE neurons during the four different RGM movements did not align with the patterns of co-modulation among MNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CCA data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The patterns of co-modulation among AE neurons during the four different RGM movements, as well as the patterns of co-modulation among MNs during observation, were more variable from trial to trial than were the patterns of MN co-modulation during execution.
source: These findings suggest that the patterns of co-modulation among AE neurons during the four different RGM movements, as well as the patterns of co-modulation among MNs during observation, were more variable from trial to trial than were the patterns of MN co-modulation during execution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the within-group alignment data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The greater trial-to-trial variability in co-modulation of MNs during observation, and even greater variability in AE neurons during execution, likely contribute to the weaker alignment of MN observation segments with MN execution segments and even weaker alignment of AE and MN execution segments.
source: This greater trial-to-trial variability in co-modulation of MNs during observation, and even greater variability in AE neurons during execution (Figure 8D), likely contribute to the weaker alignment of MN observation segments with MN execution segments and even weaker alignment of AE and MN execution segments (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: The predominant patterns of co-modulation among MNs during the four different RGM movements were relatively consistent.
source: Whereas the predominant patterns of co-modulation among MNs during the four different RGM movements were relatively consistent, co-modulation among MNs during observation was less consistent, and co-modulation of AE neurons during execution even less so.
evidence: This is supported by the within-group alignment data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Co-modulation among MNs during observation was less consistent than during execution.
source: Whereas the predominant patterns of co-modulation among MNs during the four different RGM movements were relatively consistent, co-modulation among MNs during observation was less consistent, and co-modulation of AE neurons during execution even less so.
evidence: This is supported by the within-group alignment data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Co-modulation of AE neurons during execution was even less consistent than MN co-modulation during observation.
source: Whereas the predominant patterns of co-modulation among MNs during the four different RGM movements were relatively consistent, co-modulation among MNs during observation was less consistent, and co-modulation of AE neurons during execution even less so.
evidence: This is supported by the within-group alignment data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Previous studies of reaching movements have shown that the low-dimensional population trajectories of PMd and M1 neurons occupy one subspace during a preparatory delay epoch and then transition to a different subspace during the reaching movement per se.
source: Previous studies of reaching movements have shown that the low-dimensional population trajectories of PMd and M1 neurons occupy one subspace during a preparatory delay epoch and then transition to a different subspace during the reaching movement per se (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The low-dimensional trajectories of neuronal activity controlling hand movements are relatively complex compared to reaching movements.
source: Compared to reaching movements, however, the low-dimensional trajectories of neuronal activity controlling hand movements are relatively complex (Rouse and Schieber, 2018; Suresh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The instantaneous, condition-dependent subspace of PM MN populations shifts progressively during both execution and observation of RGM trials.
source: Using this approach, we found that the instantaneous, condition-dependent subspace of PM MN populations shifts progressively during both execution and observation of RGM trials.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data in Figure 4.

claim: The instantaneous subspace of AE neuron populations shifts progressively during action execution.
source: The instantaneous subspace of AE neuron populations likewise shifts progressively during action execution.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data in Figure 4I-L.

claim: This progressive shifting of the instantaneous subspace resembles that found previously using fractional overlap of condition-dependent variance in M1 neuron populations performing a similar RGM task without a delay epoch.
source: This progressive shifting of the instantaneous subspace resembles that found previously using fractional overlap of condition-dependent variance in M1 neuron populations performing a similar RGM task without a delay epoch (Rouse and Schieber, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Short bursts of 'signal' related discharge occur in a substantial fraction of PMd neurons beginning at latencies of ~60 ms following an instructional stimulus.
source: Short bursts of 'signal' related discharge are known to occur in a substantial fraction of PMd neurons beginning at latencies of ~60 ms following an instructional stimulus (Weinrich et al., 1984; Cisek and Kalaska, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The firing rates of MNs in both PMv and PMd modulate during preparatory delay periods.
source: The firing rates of MNs in both PMv and PMd have been shown previously to modulate during preparatory delay periods (Cisek and Kalaska, 2004; Maranesi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: During execution of a reaching task, condition-dependent subspaces during the preparatory delay are orthogonal to those found during the subsequent movement epochs.
source: During execution of a reaching task, condition-dependent subspaces during the preparatory delay are orthogonal to those found during the subsequent movement epochs (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: During the preparatory delay epoch of the present RGM task, the condition-dependent, instantaneous subspace did not remain orthogonal to that which would be present at movement onset or during the movement epoch.
source: Here, we found that during the preparatory delay epoch of the present RGM task, the condition-dependent, instantaneous subspace did not remain orthogonal to that which would be present at movement onset or during the movement epoch.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data in Figure 4.

claim: As the preparatory delay proceeded, the instantaneous subspace shifted concurrently toward both the subspace that would be present at the time of the go cue ending the preparatory delay (G) and that which would be present at movement onset (M).
source: Rather, as the preparatory delay proceeded, the instantaneous subspace shifted concurrently toward both the subspace that would be present at the time of the go cue ending the preparatory delay (G) and that which would be present at movement onset (M).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: By time G, the instantaneous subspace had already shifted approximately halfway toward the time M subspace.
source: By time G, the instantaneous subspace had already shifted approximately halfway toward the time M subspace.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by the data in Figure 4C.

claim: The difference in the orthogonality of preparatory versus movement subspaces may reflect differences in reaching without grasping versus the present RGM movements.
source: This difference in the orthogonality of preparatory versus movement subspaces may reflect differences in reaching without grasping, which involves coordinated motion in 4 DOFs at the shoulder and elbow, versus the present RGM movements, which involve simultaneous, fluidly coordinated motion in at least 22 DOFs of the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and digits (Rouse and Schieber, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings and a citation to prior work.

claim: The progressive shift toward the subspace present at the onset of the final hold (H) began only after the delay period had ended (G) and around the time of movement onset (M).
source: Finally, we note that the progressive shift toward the subspace present at the onset of the final hold (H) did begin only after the delay period had ended (G) and around the time of movement onset (M).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by the data in Figure 4D.

claim: In general, instantaneous execution subspaces were distinct from instantaneous observation subspaces.
source: In general, instantaneous execution subspaces were distinct from instantaneous observation subspaces, indicated by the continuously large principal angles between them (Figure 7) and by low classification accuracy when execution trajectories were cross-projected into observation subspaces and vice versa (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Progressive shifting of the instantaneous, condition-dependent subspace was absent both in the principal angles between execution and observation subspaces and in the decoding of execution trajectory segments cross-projected into observation subspaces (and vice versa).
source: Moreover, in all three monkeys, progressive shifting of the instantaneous, condition-dependent subspace was absent both in the principal angles between execution and observation subspaces and in the decoding of execution trajectory segments cross-projected into observation subspaces (and vice versa).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The predominant modes of co-modulation among PM MNs are largely distinct during execution and observation.
source: These findings indicate that the predominant modes of co-modulation among PM MNs are largely distinct during execution and observation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 7.

claim: The present findings are consistent with recent studies that have emphasized the considerable fraction of neurons with noncongruent activity, as well as differences in neural population activity during action execution versus action observation.
source: Although MNs originally were thought to provide highly congruent neural representations of action execution and action observation (Gallese et al., 1996; Rizzolatti et al., 1996), the present findings are consistent with recent studies that have emphasized the considerable fraction of neurons with noncongruent activity, as well as differences in neural population activity during action execution versus action observation (Jiang et al., 2020; Pomper et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies and the study's own findings.

claim: The minimal overlap found in instantaneous execution and observation subspaces would be consistent with a low degree of congruence in PM MN populations.
source: Nevertheless, the minimal overlap we found in instantaneous execution and observation subspaces would be consistent with a low degree of congruence in our PM MN populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Monkey T's PM MN population may have included a substantial proportion of congruent neurons.
source: Although our microelectrode arrays were placed in similar cortical locations in the three monkeys, by chance, monkey T's PM MN population may have included a substantial proportion of congruent neurons.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that monkey T showed more overlap between execution and observation subspaces than the other monkeys.

claim: Alignment was poorest for instruction segments, somewhat higher for go segments, and strongest for movement and hold segments.
source: In all cases, alignment was poorest for instruction segments, somewhat higher for go segments, and strongest for movement and hold segments (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The progressive increase in alignment likely reflects a progressive increase in the difference between average neuron firing rates for trials involving different objects relative to the trial-by-trial variance in firing rate for a given object.
source: This progressive increase in alignment likely reflects a progressive increase in the difference between average neuron firing rates for trials involving different objects (Figure 5) relative to the trial-by-trial variance in firing rate for a given object.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figures 5 and 8C.

claim: Corresponding neural representations of action execution and observation during task epochs with higher neural firing rates have been described previously in PMd MNs and in PMv MNs using representational similarity analysis.
source: Corresponding neural representations of action execution and observation during task epochs with higher neural firing rates have been described previously in PMd MNs and in PMv MNs using representational similarity analysis (Papadourakis and Raos, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: During force production in eight different directions, neural trajectories of PMd neurons draw similar 'clocks' during execution, cooperative execution, and passive observation.
source: And during force production in eight different directions, neural trajectories of PMd neurons draw similar 'clocks' during execution, cooperative execution, and passive observation (Pezzulo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Alignment between trajectory segments of the same PM MN population during execution versus observation in the same session was less than that found between MN execution segments from two different sessions in the same monkey.
source: Alignment between trajectory segments of the same PM MN population during execution versus observation in the same session, however, was less than that found between MN execution segments from two different sessions in the same monkey.
evidence: This is supported by comparing the data in Figure 8C (red vs. black).

claim: The lower alignment between execution and observation may reflect the lower firing rates of PM MNs typically found during observation as compared to execution trials.
source: In part, this may reflect the lower firing rates of PM MNs typically found during observation as compared to execution trials (Ferroni et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The lower alignment between execution and observation may reflect more trial-by-trial variability in MN observation segments than in MN execution segments.
source: Alternatively, the lower alignment may reflect more trial-by-trial variability in MN observation segments than in MN execution segments, as indicated by the limited within-group alignment of MN observation trajectory segments (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is speculation supported by the data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: During action execution, MNs carry a consistent forward model of the intended movement, while AE neurons carry more variable feedback information.
source: Together with our previous finding that modulation of MNs leads that of non-MNs in time—both at the single neuron level and at the population level (Mazurek and Schieber, 2019)—this difference in consistency versus variability leads us to speculate that, during action execution, MNs carry a consistent forward model of the intended movement, while AE neurons carry more variable feedback information.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings and a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The common finding that large fractions of neurons in both PM and M1 discharge both during execution and during observation makes it unlikely that the discharge of MNs during observation is vestigial, with no meaning for the organism.
source: Nevertheless, the common finding that large fractions of neurons in both PM and M1 discharge both during execution and during observation makes it unlikely that the discharge of MNs during observation is vestigial, with no meaning for the organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the prevalence of mirror neurons.

claim: During observation trials the PM MN population was processing information on the sequential epochs of the behavioral task, as well as the object to which the experimenter's actions were directed on each trial.
source: Though perhaps not following the experimenter's movements closely with eye movements, or even with covert visual attention, the present results in and of themselves demonstrate that during observation trials the PM MN population was processing information on the sequential epochs of the behavioral task (Mazurek et al., 2018), as well as the object to which the experimenter's actions were directed on each trial.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and a citation to prior work.

claim: The PM MN population predictively represents the sequence of behavioral events during observation trials.
source: These findings are consistent with the notion that the PM MN population predictively represents the sequence of behavioral events during observation trials (Kilner et al., 2007; Maranesi et al., 2014; Ferroni et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior studies and the study's findings.

claim: In addition to any consistent, predictive, forward model of the observed experimenter's expected performance, MNs may also receive visual input that incorporates more variable, trial-by-trial deviation from the predicted performance being observed.
source: Our finding that within-group alignment of MN observation trajectory segments was lower than that of MN execution segments (Figure 8D), however, indicates more trial-by-trial variability of MN co-modulation during observation than during execution. In addition to any consistent, predictive, forward model of the observed experimenter's expected performance, MNs thus may also receive visual input that incorporates more variable, trial-by-trial deviation from the predicted performance being observed.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings shown in Figure 8D.

claim: One classic interpretation of similar latent dynamics in the PM MN population during execution and observation would be that this similarity provides a means for the brain to recognize similar movements performed by the monkey during execution and by the experimenter during observation.
source: One classic interpretation of similar latent dynamics in the PM MN population during execution and observation would be that this similarity provides a means for the brain to recognize similar movements performed by the monkey during execution and by the experimenter during observation.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional interpretation of the findings.

claim: PM MN population activity during action observation may represent different movements one might execute oneself in response to those made by another individual.
source: Alternatively, given that observation of another individual can be considered a form of social interaction, PM MN population activity during action observation, rather than representing movements made by another individual similar to one's own movements, instead may represent different movements one might execute oneself in response to those made by another individual (Ninomiya et al., 2020; Bonini et al., 2022; Ferrucci et al., 2022; Pomper et al., 2023).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The neural dynamics of PM MN populations are more similar during observation of biological versus non-biological movements than during execution versus observation.
source: This possibility is consistent with the finding that the neural dynamics of PM MN populations are more similar during observation of biological versus non-biological movements than during execution versus observation (Albertini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The similar relative organization of the execution and observation population activity in PM MNs revealed by alignment of their latent dynamics through CCA could constitute a correspondence between particular movements that might be made by the subject in response to particular movements made by the other individual.
source: Though neurons active only during observation of others (AO units) have been hypothesized to drive observation activity in MNs, the present AO populations were too small to analyze with the approaches we applied here. Nevertheless, the similar relative organization of the execution and observation population activity in PM MNs revealed here by alignment of their latent dynamics through CCA could constitute a correspondence between particular movements that might be made by the subject in response to particular movements made by the other individual, i.e., responsive movements which would not necessarily be motorically similar to the observed movements.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: Other studies that have not separated the condition-dependent versus condition-independent variance in neural activity have described even more similar latent dynamics during execution and observation.
source: Other studies that have not separated the condition-dependent versus condition-independent variance in neural activity have described even more similar latent dynamics during execution and observation (Mazurek et al., 2018; Jerjian et al., 2020; Pezzulo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Condition-dependent activity may represent particular types of movement in a manner that differs depending on the actor (one's self versus another individual).
source: We speculate that condition-dependent activity may represent particular types of movement (e.g. sphere, button, coaxial cylinder, or perpendicular cylinder) in a manner that differs depending on the actor (one's self versus another individual).
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: Condition-independent activity may provide a neural representation of a class of action independent of the actor.
source: Concurrently, condition-independent activity may provide a neural representation of a class of action (e.g. RGM movements) independent of the actor.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings.
